After nearly four decades as a high-tempo investigative journalist, Jeff Lee found an unexpected teacher in the most unlikely of places: his backyard beehives. What began as a hobby after his wife's unusual encounter with a "beard of bees" at a Vancouver science exhibition gradually transformed into a complete life reorientation. The bees, Lee discovered, had little patience for his frenetic newsroom habits—they stung him repeatedly until he learned to slow down, listen, and work at their pace rather than his own.
Facing burnout and potential redundancy at the Vancouver Sun in his late fifties, Lee made a bold choice. Instead of simply retiring, he and his wife Amanda moved 300 miles east to rural British Columbia to purchase an actual bee farm. The transition wasn't smooth—they lost nearly all their bees in the first two years—but they persisted, slowly rebuilding to 800 hives and earning awards at major US honey shows. Lee's journey into journalism had itself been accidental, beginning with a lumber mill injury and bar work that led him to freelance writing, but beekeeping represented something more intentional: a conscious decision to reshape not just his work, but his entire approach to living.
This story resonates because it challenges conventional notions of career arcs and retirement. Lee's experience suggests that reinvention is possible at any age, and that sometimes the best teachers come with stingers. His bees demanded he abandon the "crash and bang" mentality that had defined his professional life, offering in return not just honey, but a fundamentally calmer, more present way of being in the world—one that made him, as he puts it, "a better human being."

item.title: Country diary: Teasing out spiders with a tuning fork | Susie White
item.description:
In the elegant surroundings of an Edwardian bandstand, a small group gathered for an unusual lesson: a guided walk into the world of spiders. Led by Fran Garcia of the British Arachnological Society, the expedition combined scientific curiosity with playful teaching methods that captivated both adults and children alike. Using wire, rope, glue, and even a folding knife to illustrate spider anatomy and web construction, Garcia transformed what might have been a dry lecture into an engaging hands-on experience.
The real magic unfolded as the group ventured into the field. At an old brick wall, Garcia demonstrated how laceweb spiders detect prey by striking a tuning fork against the stonework and holding it near their silken tunnels. The vibration lured a spider from its lair—a dark leg appearing, then a quick rush forward before the creature realized the deception and retreated. Among creeping thistles, Garcia pulled out a spray bottle and misted the vegetation, instantly revealing hidden webs in shimmering droplets, recreating the beauty of a dewy morning. Along the way, participants learned to distinguish true spiders from their arachnid cousins, the harvestmen, and examined a delicate wasp spider egg sac slowly making its way northward with climate shifts.
This story offers a quiet reminder that wonder lives in overlooked corners, waiting for someone with curiosity and a tuning fork to coax it into view. For one young participant, childhood spider fears dissolved in the absorption of truly seeing these small architects at work.

item.title: Kaikohe's long-awaited community hub and library opens its doors
item.description:
After 15 years of planning and anticipation, the town of Kaikohe in New Zealand's Far North has opened Te Kākahu, a $14.8 million community hub and library that aims to revitalize the town center and provide a creative gathering space for residents of all ages. The complex goes well beyond a traditional library, featuring a council service center, meeting rooms, a gaming room, a podcast studio, and a café. Perhaps most notably, it includes a creativity room equipped with modern making tools—3D printers, laser cutters, screen printers, and sewing machines—inviting locals to learn, create, and experiment.
The opening drew busloads of excited schoolchildren and residents eager to explore the new facility on Broadway and Raihara Street. Nine-year-old Atutahi Ritchie, visiting with her school, was particularly enthusiastic about the badge-making and 3D printing stations. Far North Deputy Mayor Chicky Rudkin celebrated the hub as a long-overdue asset for Kaikohe, emphasizing that it would serve everyone from children to elders, providing both quiet spaces and active areas for connection and creativity. The 22-year-old project manager, Hori Tane, described his own journey managing the build and expressed hope that the hub would offer young people a safe place to gather and grow.
What makes this story quietly remarkable is the patience and persistence it represents—15 years of community dreaming, designing with input from local schools and hapū, and building with local contractors. Te Kākahu is more than infrastructure; it's an investment in pride, connection, and the creative potential of a town that has been waiting for a space to call its own gathering heart.

item.title: A glimmer of good news for Britain's sleepy dormouse
item.description:
After decades of decline, Britain's hazel dormouse may finally be staging a modest comeback. New monitoring data suggests the population of these beloved small mammals increased by nearly 10% between 2020 and 2025, offering conservationists a rare glimmer of hope. The hazel dormouse, once common across England and Wales, has vanished from roughly 20 counties as woodlands and hedgerows have disappeared, with overall numbers plummeting almost 60% since 2000.
The recent uptick coincides with a stretch of warmer, drier springs and summers, conditions researchers believe may be helping dormice thrive. These famously sleepy creatures hibernate from October through May and even enter torpor—brief periods of deep sleep—during chilly or wet summer days when food is scarce. Warmer weather appears to reduce their need for torpor, giving them more active time to feed, build fat reserves, and potentially raise additional litters. It's a striking example of how shifting climate patterns can reshape the fortunes of a species in unexpected ways.
Yet conservationists urge caution. The population remains far below historical levels, and many questions linger about how dormice will cope with warmer, wetter winters and other long-term climate shifts. Protecting the woodlands and hedgerows these animals depend on remains essential. This story matters because it captures both the fragility and resilience of wildlife in a changing world—a reminder that even small improvements are worth celebrating, while acknowledging the hard work still ahead to ensure these enchanting sleepers don't slip away for good.

item.title: This is Fantástico — Manila Norte: the cemetery of the living
item.description:
In Manila Norte, one of the Philippines' largest cemeteries, an extraordinary community has taken shape: approximately six thousand living residents share space with a million graves. Families have made their homes among the tombstones and mausoleums, transforming what was meant as a resting place for the dead into an improvised neighborhood for the living. This unusual arrangement isn't a choice born of eccentricity, but rather a stark illustration of the housing crisis affecting urban centers worldwide.
Brazilian news program Fantástico sent a team to document daily life in this cemetery community, exploring what it means to grow up, work, and fall in love surrounded by graves. The report follows an earlier investigation into Hong Kong's notorious "coffin apartments," where extreme housing shortages have forced residents into living spaces barely larger than a bed. The Manila Norte story adds another dimension to understanding how millions navigate impossible housing markets in densely populated cities.
What makes this story quietly remarkable is its human focus. Rather than treating the cemetery residents as curiosities, the reporting team sought to understand the textures of everyday life in such an unconventional setting. The accompanying podcast features conversations with the producers about what surprised them most during their time in Manila Norte. It's a story that asks us to consider how housing insecurity shapes communities in unexpected ways, and how people create homes and build lives even in the most unlikely places.
